title: Why Dominance Does Not Spread an Allele

scenes.tts: A dominant allele shows its trait whenever a person carries it. Why does it not spread until nearly everyone carries it? Follow the allele copies, not just the visible trait. Their count will expose the answer.
scenes.caption: A dominant allele shows its trait whenever a person carries it. Why does it not spread until nearly everyone carries it? Follow the allele copies, not just the visible trait. Their count will expose the answer.
scenes.visual: THE WORLD AND COLOUR MAP, kept throughout both films: allele A is BLUE; allele a is GOLD; people are pale-grey rounded outlines; a force acting on the population is RED; expected values and guides are WHITE; uncertainty or chance motion is TEAL. Dark background. A large row of pale-grey people fills two-thirds of the frame. Each holds two blocks, blue A or gold a. Above them, blue outlines mark everyone carrying A, so both AA and Aa look alike. A small label marks the starting people 'already at Hardy-Weinberg proportions'. A dashed WHITE ghost bar labelled 'predicted?' rises toward 'everyone' across three schematic generations, while the actual visible blue group stays the same size in each generation, under the question 'Why not everyone?'. Beneath them a WHITE-outlined blue-gold allele-frequency bar stays fixed in all three generations. Blocks keep bobbing gently.
scenes.narration: A dominant allele shows its trait whenever a person carries it. Why does it not spread until nearly everyone carries it? Follow the allele copies, not just the visible trait. Their count will expose the answer.

scenes.visual: Title 'Why Dominance Does Not Spread an Allele' appears over the same moving people for two seconds. The question remains faintly behind it; allele blocks continue a slow vertical bob.

scenes.tts: Each person holds a genotype, an allele pair at one locus. Population genetics asks a different question. Across everyone, what fraction of all copies are blue? That fraction is an allele frequency. An individual cannot supply that population-wide fraction.
scenes.caption: Each person holds a genotype, an allele pair at one locus. Population genetics asks a different question. Across everyone, what fraction of all copies are blue? That fraction is an allele frequency. An individual cannot supply that population-wide fraction.
scenes.visual: The people slide into one row. Their paired blocks detach and flow upward into a wide transparent pool. A bracket labels one person's pair 'genotype'. A wide bracket around every block reads 'population allele copies'. A blue share bar grows beneath the pool and is labelled 'frequency of A = p'; the gold remainder is labelled 'frequency of a = q'. Display p = 0.60 and q = 0.40 only on screen.
scenes.narration: Each person holds a genotype, an allele pair at one locus. Population genetics asks a different question. Across everyone, what fraction of all copies are blue? That fraction is an allele frequency. An individual cannot supply that population-wide fraction.

scenes.tts: The pool contains blue copies and gold copies. Their fractions are called pee and cue. Together they fill the pool. Dominance changes which pairs show a trait, but it adds no blue copies. The pool measures inheritance, not outward appearance.
scenes.caption: The pool contains blue copies and gold copies. Their fractions are called p and q. Together they fill the pool. Dominance changes which pairs show a trait, but it adds no blue copies. The pool measures inheritance, not outward appearance.
scenes.visual: The carried pool fills most of the frame. Blue and gold blocks circulate slowly without changing count. The p and q bar locks to the pool inventory. Below, AA and Aa pair cards both glow blue for the dominant phenotype, while aa stays gold. A counter beside the pool does not move. A small label reads 'same copies'.
scenes.narration: The pool contains blue copies and gold copies. Their fractions are called p and q. Together they fill the pool. Dominance changes which pairs show a trait, but it adds no blue copies. The pool measures inheritance, not outward appearance.

scenes.tts: Now let eggs and sperm pair at random. Before they pair, predict the next blue fraction. Does random pairing increase it, decrease it, or leave it unchanged? Keep your eye on the copies.
scenes.caption: Now let eggs and sperm pair at random. Before they pair, predict the next blue fraction. Does random pairing increase it, decrease it, or leave it unchanged? Keep your eye on the copies.
scenes.visual: The pool separates into an egg lane and a sperm lane, each carrying the same blue-gold split. Three possible result bars appear large across the bottom: blue share higher, lower, or unchanged. The prompt 'What happens to p?' sits above them. Blocks drift toward pairing gates but do not enter.
scenes.narration: Now let eggs and sperm pair at random. Before they pair, predict the next blue fraction. Does random pairing increase it, decrease it, or leave it unchanged? Keep your eye on the copies.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. The three possible bars and 'What happens to p?' remain. Blue and gold blocks drift slowly in both lanes; the pairing gates shimmer without admitting blocks.

scenes.tts: Random means each draw follows the pool's current mix. Draw blue from both lanes, and the pair is a blue homozygote. Draw unlike colours, in either order, and the pair is heterozygous. Draw gold from both, and the pair is a gold homozygote. No draw remembers which phenotype carried a copy.
scenes.caption: Random means each draw follows the pool's current mix. Draw blue from both lanes, and the pair is a blue homozygote. Draw unlike colours, in either order, and the pair is heterozygous. Draw gold from both, and the pair is a gold homozygote. No draw remembers which phenotype carried a copy.
scenes.visual: The lanes become the top and left edges of a large probability square. Moving cursors select one block from each edge. The blue-blue cell fills first and is labelled 'AA'. The two blue-gold cells fill next and merge visually under 'Aa'. The gold-gold cell fills last under 'aa'. Areas use the displayed p = 0.60 and q = 0.40 and are computed, not schematic.
scenes.narration: Random means each draw follows the pool's current mix. Draw blue from both lanes, and the pair is a blue homozygote. Draw unlike colours, in either order, and the pair is heterozygous. Draw gold from both, and the pair is a gold homozygote. No draw remembers which phenotype carried a copy.

scenes.tts: The square gives the expected Hardy-Weinberg genotype proportions. Blue homozygotes occupy pee squared. Heterozygotes occupy both mixed regions. Gold homozygotes occupy cue squared. Together the regions fill the whole next generation. These areas describe people, not new allele copies.
scenes.caption: The square gives the expected Hardy-Weinberg genotype proportions. Blue homozygotes occupy p squared. Heterozygotes occupy both mixed regions. Gold homozygotes occupy q squared. Together the regions fill the whole next generation. These areas describe people, not new allele copies.
scenes.visual: Keep the computed square large. Each region pulses as its on-screen expression appears: p², pq, qp, q². The two mixed regions slide together and their labels transform into 2pq. A side label reads 'genotype proportions'. The unchanged blue-gold allele bar stays visible above the square.
scenes.narration: The square gives the expected Hardy-Weinberg genotype proportions. Blue homozygotes occupy p squared. Heterozygotes occupy both mixed regions. Gold homozygotes occupy q squared. Together the regions fill the whole next generation. These areas describe people, not new allele copies.

scenes.tts: Recount blue copies in the new people. Every blue homozygote contributes only blue. Every mixed pair contributes half blue. Together those shares return exactly to pee. Random mating changed the pairings, not the allele frequency.
scenes.caption: Recount blue copies in the new people. Every blue homozygote contributes only blue. Every mixed pair contributes half blue. Together those shares return exactly to p. Random mating changed the pairings, not the allele frequency.
scenes.visual: The square breaks into genotype cards, then every card opens and releases its two blocks. Blue blocks stream into a new bar; gold blocks fill the rest. On screen, p² + pq transforms into p(p + q), then into p. The new bar slides under the original and matches it exactly. The 'unchanged' prediction receives a white outline.
scenes.narration: Recount blue copies in the new people. Every blue homozygote contributes only blue. Every mixed pair contributes half blue. Together those shares return exactly to p. Random mating changed the pairings, not the allele frequency.

scenes.tts: Dominance still changes the visible count. Both blue homozygotes and heterozygotes show the dominant trait. Yet visibility is not transmission advantage. A visible effect is not a copying mechanism. Without unequal survival, reproduction, or another force, blue copies receive no extra route forward.
scenes.caption: Dominance still changes the visible count. Both blue homozygotes and heterozygotes show the dominant trait. Yet visibility is not transmission advantage. A visible effect is not a copying mechanism. Without unequal survival, reproduction, or another force, blue copies receive no extra route forward.
scenes.visual: Return to the row of people. AA and Aa outlines glow BLUE while aa stays GOLD. A large eye icon counts visible trait holders; beside it, the allele bar remains fixed. A proposed blue shortcut arrow toward the next generation appears, then fades because no force acts. No block is removed or duplicated.
scenes.narration: Dominance still changes the visible count. Both blue homozygotes and heterozygotes show the dominant trait. Yet visibility is not transmission advantage. A visible effect is not a copying mechanism. Without unequal survival, reproduction, or another force, blue copies receive no extra route forward.

scenes.tts: This is a baseline, not a claim that real populations are motionless. It assumes a large population, random mating at this locus, and no force changing the copy pool. Hardy-Weinberg predicts genotype counts. It turns no-force reasoning into a testable expectation. Data can then depart from that expectation.
scenes.caption: This is a baseline, not a claim that real populations are motionless. It assumes a large population, random mating at this locus, and no force changing the copy pool. Hardy-Weinberg predicts genotype counts. It turns no-force reasoning into a testable expectation. Data can then depart from that expectation.
scenes.visual: The genotype square becomes three expected-count bars labelled AA, Aa, and aa. A second set of observed bars rises beside them but remains unlabeled as fitting or departing. A bracket labels the white bars 'null expectation'. Around the allele pool, badges for selection, migration, mutation, and drift remain outside a dashed boundary. Everything is marked 'schematic' except the computed square.
scenes.narration: This is a baseline, not a claim that real populations are motionless. It assumes a large population, random mating at this locus, and no force changing the copy pool. Hardy-Weinberg predicts genotype counts. It turns no-force reasoning into a testable expectation. Data can then depart from that expectation.

scenes.tts: So answer the opening question by counting copies. Mating reshuffles alleles; dominance alone does not change their frequency. A changing allele bar requires something that changes which copies enter the next generation.
scenes.caption: So answer the opening question by counting copies. Mating reshuffles alleles; dominance alone does not change their frequency. A changing allele bar requires something that changes which copies enter the next generation.
scenes.visual: The people, pool, square, and matched before-and-after bars align into one vertical story. A RED force arrow approaches the bar but pauses before touching it. The fixed boundary between blue and gold glows. On the rule, the words 'mating reshuffles' appear over rotating pairs while 'frequency unchanged' anchors the bar.
scenes.narration: So answer the opening question by counting copies. Mating reshuffles alleles; dominance alone does not change their frequency. A changing allele bar requires something that changes which copies enter the next generation.

scenes.visual: End card over the dimmed allele pool. Show one centred line only: 'Mating reshuffles alleles; dominance alone does not change their frequency.' Blue and gold blocks continue drifting gently behind it.
